epub_9.title: The Sartorial Riches of the Silent-Film Era
epub_9.text:
The Sartorial Riches of the Silent-Film Era
Goings On
The Sartorial Riches of the Silent-Film Era
Also: the neo-soul of Erykah Badu, a festival of Indian classical dance, John Wilson’s ode to concrete, and more.
By Rachel Syme,Dan Stahl,Sheldon Pearce,Marina Harss,Brian Seibert,Richard Brody,Taran Dugal
September 11, 2026
In today’s world
of rumbling, thunderous Dolby surround sound, the concept of silent cinema can feel very distant. Sure, you can catch a replay of “Metropolis” or “City Lights” every now and then at Film Forum—and you can listen to Karina Longworth’s excellent podcast about Hollywood history, “You Must Remember This”—but there are notably few other opportunities to dip one’s toes into the era before talkies arrived. As such,
“
Goddesses in the Machine: Fashion in American Silent Film
,”
a new exhibition opening on Sept. 18, at the Bard Graduate Center, on the Upper West Side, is a welcome event.
The show surveys the many fashion designers, including Lady Duff-Gordon, Lilian St. Cyr, Natacha Rambova, Travis Banton, and Salvatore Ferragamo, who brought their sartorial talents to the silent screen. It includes showings of several serial dramas from the nineteen-tens, including “The Perils of Pauline,” from 1914; “The Whirl of Life,” from 1915; and “The Mysterious Airman,” from 1928, all with live accompaniment by the pianist Makia Matsumura. The costume designers for these movies made clothes that spoke loudly when leading ladies could not; there is a sumptuous drama to the pieces they created which echoes through time.—
Rachel Syme
About Town
Off Broadway
“What they don’t tell you about Nashville, Tennessee / Is heartbreak’s the only thing they hand out for free,” an aspiring country singer-songwriter wails in
“
Music City
,”
a toe-tappin’, hand-clappin’, tissue-dabbin’ humdinger of a show. If some of J. T. Harding’s tunes sound familiar, it’s because they were originally sung by the likes of Blake Shelton and Keith Urban. But they’ve been blessed with a book so smooth, by Peter Zinn, that they fit right into this story of three hardscrabble youngsters chasing country-music dreams at almost any cost. Clifton Chadick’s set plops you smack dab in the center of the action, at a table in a bar on open-mike night. With right fine actin’, singin’, playin’, or other carryin’ on by most everyone onstage.—
Dan Stahl (St. Luke’s Theatre; through Sept. 19.)
Off Broadway
The magician Jamie Allan’s
“
Amaze
”
is a show for kids—and for adults who’d unironically describe themselves as “kids at heart.” As a critic at heart, I tired of Allan’s eager-beaver affect, though it has the advantage of putting audience participants at ease. His artful tricks are organized around a narrative of his development as a magician, from the Fisher-Price magic kit he got as a boy to a hybrid analog-digital sleight of hand that landed him on BBC One. But the razzle-dazzle pairs oddly with his earnestness, as do the video projections with antique furnishings. And what would Freud make of his wife performing alongside him in the “glamorous assistant” role he originally promised his mother?—
D.S. (New World Stages; open run.)
Soul
Long before “woke” was co-opted and turned into a dog whistle, it operated as a perfect word to describe the music and artistry of
Erykah Badu
. “I stay woke,” she sang on the 2008 song “Master Teacher,” using a term originally meant to characterize not just a greater level of social awareness but a state of being, as she put it, in alignment with nature. Both are core ideals for the neo-soul movement, of which she is a pioneer, whose sound is as earthy and robust as it is conscious. A well-known sage of modern blues and psychedelic R. & B., Badu continues her eternal vision quest on a new album with the prolific beat-making heavyweight the Alchemist, and both are joined in concert by the similarly woke-minded hip-hop group De La Soul.—
Sheldon Pearce (
Forest Hills Stadium
; Sept. 18.)
Dance
Erasing Borders Dance Festival
encompasses a wide palette of Indian classical dance—officially, there are eight forms, but in reality there are many more. Kuchipudi—light, airy, rhythmic—originated in Andhra Pradesh, where it was performed by men, as part of mythological dance dramas. Now it is mainly performed by women. Here, a kuchipudi solo by Sreelakshmy Kallungal Govardhanan, who moves with an almost feral power, displays dramatic abilities—central to kuchipudi—that transcend linguistic barriers. A trio led by Shila Mehta performs kathak, a more abstract dance style from the north; others perform odissi (from Odisha) and the swaying mohiniyattam (Kerala). There will even be a bit of contemporary dance, still based in South Asian technique, performed by Preeti Vasudevan.—
Marina Harss (Kaye Playhouse; Sept. 19-20.)
Dance
This year’s iteration of City Center’s popular
Fall for Dance Festival
offers the standard mix of the promising and the poorly chosen, the not-so-familiar and the all-too. The most intriguing première comes from Robbie Fairchild, a former New York City Ballet star who has found success on Broadway and on the West End. His piece “Lord Chamberlain’s Men” finds an emotional backstory for the forbidden-love theme of “Romeo and Juliet” in the amatory sonnets that Shakespeare wrote to a young man. Other festival highlights include Juan Tomás de la Molía, an on-the-rise flamenco dancer of fresh musicality, and Miami City Ballet, with a new Alexei Ratmansky piece set to Strauss waltzes.—
Brian Seibert (New York City Center; Sept. 22-Oct. 3.)
Movies
Following the method of his HBO series “How To with John Wilson,” the Queens-based local explorer offers his first feature film,
“The History of Concrete,”
a warmhearted, wide-rangingly inquisitive documentary about the peculiar implications of the ubiquitous substance. It involves literal cinematic shoegaze—an encounter with a New York contractor who blasts away chewing-gum stains on a sidewalk—and takes Wilson to a primordial concrete road in small-town Ohio, a concrete convention in Las Vegas, and even the concrete-domed Pantheon in Rome. He ponders his own method, because his central theme is the emotional side of the material city, where a tight-knit group of runners pounds the pavement and a do-it-yourself repair job reminds him that even the intimacy of home involves a throng of connections.—
Richard Brody (Opening Sept. 18.)
Bar Tab
Taran Dugal finds a confessional in a Chinatown paradise.
The climb from Hell to Heaven can be long and arduous. Take Dante’s, for instance. The man persevered through nine circles of inferno, sans electrolytes, only to find himself staring up at the mountain of Purgatory.
Merda!
And you thought your walkup was a trek. Luckily for those partygoers with forbidden-fruit predilections,
Gosh,
a new guest-list-only Chinatown club (accessible via e-mail), allows patrons a quicker ascent to Paradise, if they can stomach the snooty vibe. On a recent weekend, a group of friends congregated in the venue’s basement, a narrow room with black leather couches and steel tables. Red neon tubes illuminated art works ranging from the disturbing (a black-and-white photograph of a person stuffing sausages in their mouth) to the mundane (a pastoral painting of a snowshoe-wearing rifleman). The friends ranked their drinks. The Sadomaso, a sharp fusion of Amaro Montenegro, mezcal, lemon, and sotol, placed last—far too bitter. Then came the Mirafiori, a golden, overly sweet mix of mezcal, crème de litchi, lime, and nasturtium. The Gin Basil Smash, an addictive blend of gin, lemon, sugar, and basil, topped the list. Simplicity was proportionate to success: the bar had a formidable Guinness on tap. Pints in hand, the group ascended to the ground level—an elegant Japanese-style parlor dotted with toadstool seats—but didn’t stay in that purgatory long, instead heading to the top floor, a tentlike lounge enclosed by velvet curtains printed with a psychedelic pattern of dinosaurs, naked gnomes, and Babelian monoliths. Two members of the group stumbled through a nondescript door nearby, and found a wood-panelled confessional, where an empty beer glass sat beside the divider. In this version of paradise, even angels have secrets, divulged, apparently, over a cold Irish stout.
P.S. Good stuff on the internet:
“What Walls Are Good For,” by Dick Westheimer
How to use the last of the season’s peaches
The perfect combination

epub_10.title: How a Skateboarder Sees Los Angeles
epub_10.text:
How a Skateboarder Sees Los Angeles
Photo Booth
How a Skateboarder Sees Los Angeles
Jerry Hsu captures the city’s manic extremes, with photographs of overturned cars, collisions, and a bank building ablaze.
By Hua Hsu
September 05, 2026
Jerry Hsu grew up in San Jose, about an hour south of San Francisco, and, for a time, he assumed he would never leave. He didn’t need to. In the late nineties and two-thousands, Hsu and his daredevil friends had proudly put their sleepy Silicon Valley city on the map as an unlikely skateboarding capital. He noticed that young skateboarders from around the country were moving to San Jose, “and it had to do with my group of friends and these videos we were making,” he told me. “It’s like when a random city becomes very important for some random reason. We were able to have our slice of heaven.”
The son of Taiwanese immigrants, Hsu was a precocious talent and became a professional skateboarder in his mid-teens. Magazines sent photographers to San Jose to shoot pictures of him, and he eventually became interested in their craft, what kind of gear they were using, the parallels between their respective art forms. His mother would drive him to the local Barnes & Noble, where he grew fascinated with how
Nan Goldin
and
Larry Clark
chronicled the micro-scenes around them. (She also famously procured him a concrete parking block so that he could practice tricks at home.) As skateboard companies sent him around the world in his late teens and twenties, he began obsessively taking photographs of the strange, funny, often macabre things he came across, and publishing them on Tumblr or in
Vice
magazine.
In 2011, Hsu moved to Los Angeles, primarily for a relationship, and to further his career as a skateboarder. But he also felt a private excitement about spending time photographing a city “that was more rich with things I wanted to see.” With a body thrashed by occupational hazards, Hsu, who is forty-four, orients his life nowadays around running Sci-Fi Fantasy, his skate company, and roaming the city to take pictures. His latest book, “
How About Never
,” is a brutal and wondrous chronicle of the sights he has sought out these past fifteen years.
It’s no surprise that a skateboarder, constantly scanning the landscape for surfaces to recontextualize, might see the world differently. Hsu’s photographs explore the city’s manic extremes. Some of them are quick visual gags: the symmetry of two discarded toilets stacked like yin and yang (or in a sixty-nine position) on the side of the street, a veiny sex toy that’s washed up in a brackish puddle. A triangular slab has fallen neatly out of a wall, as though it was too weary to go on. He notices signs of life where others might just perceive neglect, such as a flower bush sequestered behind a foreboding fence. One picture feels like a short story waiting to be written: a tree hollowed out by rot has been stuffed with roses by a neighbor who felt sorry for it. Hsu maps a Los Angeles of leftovers and castoffs; portraits of friends and strangers in the street are full of dazed, inscrutable expressions.
“My attraction to risk is ever present,” he explains. Hsu is the type of person who runs toward fire, as evidenced by pictures of overturned cars, collisions, a bank building ablaze. They manage to avoid feeling grimly voyeuristic. Instead, there’s a sense of stillness in these images, akin to that flash of calm after you’ve done something ruinous to your body but before your brain registers pain or begins cycling through consequences. I was drawn to a picture of a smashed car windshield, the glass frozen in a series of circular ripples, until it began to resemble the vertical slit of a reptilian eye. It was still in mind a few pages later, as I studied how a young man’s artificial eye seemed to match the orange shade of his hoodie.
My favorite picture in the book finds a sensibly blue Subaru station wagon that has somehow turned on its side in the middle of the night. There’s something funny about its vanity license plate (“
4A POEM
”) and the way the car’s headlights shine brightly on a house in the distance, as if to point attention away from itself.
Hsu says that his ex-wife often remarked that he had a sixth sense for stumbling upon bizarre, uncanny scenes. Many of his images, even the faintly violent ones, possess an absurdist humor: in one, a motorist explains to a police officer why their Toyota has hopped the curb, but, from a distance, it almost looks like the sedan is playfully trying to return to its mates in a used-car lot. Hsu explained that he finds a lot of his subjects by using
Citizen
, the incident-reporting app, to see if anything intriguing is happening nearby.
For all the book’s darkness, there are pictures that feel sublime and vast. There are numerous pictures from the hills surrounding Los Angeles where you can’t tell whether the city is on fire or merely aglow with energy. A suburban home like any other sits haloed by clouds, with California’s placid skies a screen of infinite possibility. A picture of a cat vaulting from a gate to a fence takes on an outsized feeling of hope. “Maybe this is corny,” Hsu explained to me, “but all this chaos and these little beautiful secrets I found here reminded me of myself. It was a mirror and threshold.”
I first learned about Hsu in the early two-thousands. My younger cousin wound up skating at his house a few times and excitedly asked if we were related to him. Sadly, the answer was no. Admiring Hsu’s twin careers taught me to see my own Silicon Valley suburb differently, even though I was someone who’d felt the urge to leave as soon as I could. I realized that I hadn’t tried hard enough to appreciate all the beauty and weirdness that was actually available to me.
Where Hsu’s early work was filled with the people in his life, his work over the past decade is marked by a kind of solitude. Some of “How About Never” feels uncomfortably intimate, from its opening image of a cake flower resting on a knife above a dingy sink to pictures of hospital rooms, scabs and bruises, his ex-wife resting her palms on the sink in their bathroom. Hsu says that he spent nearly ten years editing the book, and that he recently realized that it also tracks the dissolution of his marriage. As he put it, there’s a private story of “hope, despair, all the feelings that are associated with trying to make a loving relationship happen” in how the images are sequenced.
Hsu spoke to me from his home in Los Angeles, and at one point, he angled his laptop to show me a shelf full of negatives and contact sheets, and hard drives of digital photos. His archives contain nearly every picture he’s taken in the past twenty-five years, even random things he texts to his friends. He rarely deletes pictures from his phone, thinking that even the imperfect shots might be meaningful to him someday. It reminded me of the famous series of home movies that Hsu made of himself, as a teen-ager, practicing tricks in his parents’ garage. The result of all those hours of practice was a style of effortless cool. Yet he felt compelled to keep a record of all the failures and misses along the way. “Maybe because I have this type of vision, it really takes away from another type that’s more practical,” he said, laughing. A few minutes after we hung up, he got an alert on his phone: a car had just flipped over in Koreatown. ♦

How to Protect Democracy
Comment
How to Protect Democracy
The emergence of Germany’s far right as a political force represents an old dilemma.
By Joshua Yaffa
September 13, 2026
The Brandmauer, or firewall, was meant to protect German democracy. The principle arose in the mid-twenty-tens, in response to the rise of Alternative für Deutschland, or the AfD, a right-wing populist party known for its ethnonationalism, hard-line anti-immigration platform, and pro-Russian foreign policy. Germany’s traditional parties agreed to refrain from any sort of political coöperation: they would neither form coalitions with the AfD nor rely on its votes for governing majorities.
Now the Brandmauer, long under pressure, may be facing collapse. This month, in Saxony-Anhalt, a small German state of slightly more than two million people in the east, the AfD won a plurality of votes: nearly forty-four per cent. Without an outright majority, the Party can’t govern on its own, but that number is more than double the AfD’s share of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt just five years ago. And it’s the first time in Germany’s postwar history that a far-right party has come this close to governing a state.
The emergence of the AfD as a political force represents one of democracy’s oldest dilemmas: how to respond to anti-democratic movements that have a democratic base of support. A century ago, conservative politicians in the Weimar Republic made the fateful, and tragic, choice to appoint Adolf Hitler as Chancellor and to name other Nazi figures to ministerial posts, believing that they could control them by absorbing them into the governing apparatus. That turned out, well, as it turned out. In 1949, in order to prevent such a disaster from ever occurring again, Basic Law, the country’s modern constitution, enshrined a set of principles known as
wehrhafte Demokratie
, or militant democracy, which call on state institutions to mobilize against those who seek to undermine democracy from within. The Brandmauer is an informal compact, but it’s certainly within the spirit of that political culture.
This postwar consensus has found an antagonist worthy of concern in the AfD. The Holocaust, one Party leader said, was a mere “speck of bird shit” on a thousand years of German history; another described Berlin’s Holocaust Memorial as a “monument of shame.” A Party policy calling for “remigration” is vague yet tinged with menace; in 2023, senior AfD figures attended a secret conference in Potsdam to discuss mass deportations of immigrants, including what one participant deemed “non-assimilated citizens.” Whereas other European right-wing populist parties (such as the National Rally, in France) and leaders (like the Italian Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni) have drifted toward the center in an effort to make their positions more palatable, the AfD has remained resolutely illiberal. Germany’s domestic-intelligence service has classified some local branches of the Party as extremist organizations.
The Brandmauer, then, may have been a necessary instrument, but it allowed establishment parties to focus on the mechanics of defense rather than on offense—that is, on articulating a program that will win over voters. The region of the former East Germany, for example, is facing deindustrialization and demographic decline; voters there, who tend to be poorer than those in the west and feel alienated and excluded, provide the AfD with its highest levels of support.
Jana Hensel, a journalist born in East Germany, published a book this year subtitled “Why the East Is Turning Away from Democracy.” She said, “By spending all this time thinking about how to maintain the firewall, we managed to forget the voters on the other side—how they live, their feelings, their problems.” The Brandmauer allowed the AfD to enjoy the image of the disruptive outsider, the one who really feels your pain, without the responsibility of having to do anything about it.
In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD’s strong showing came at the expense of the Christian Democratic Union, the center-right party of Angela Merkel and of the current Chancellor, Friedrich Merz. The AfD hopes to persuade a handful of C.D.U. members to break from their firewall pledge and enable a governing majority; AfD leaders are also courting a far-left party that shares their hostility toward immigration and current policy on Russia and Ukraine. Perhaps more likely is a political stasis, in which neither the AfD nor the forces opposed to it take charge outright. That’s hardly a victory for those seen as the protectors of Germany’s normality.
In truth, no mainstream German party has figured out a formula for slowing the AfD’s electoral march. Merz has periodically flirted with adopting part of its agenda, specifically on immigration. Last year, in a controversial vote in the Bundestag, the C.D.U. pushed through a resolution on stricter migration rules which it knew would gain a majority only with AfD support. But one study after another shows that, when established parties take on the policies of the insurgent right, they end up just shedding more votes to it. In recent days, some C.D.U. members have renewed talk of a legal ban of the AfD. None of these stopgap measures deal with the real problem: like much of Europe, Germany is changing—economically, culturally, politically—and, in a sizable part of the population, that is stoking a desire for radical solutions. “Even if the AfD won’t fix the problems of its supporters,” Hensel said, “it will destroy the system under which they think they have suffered.”
Two other German states have elections later this month, and in 2029 the country will hold federal elections that will seat a new Bundestag and, perhaps, a new Chancellor. The AfD is rising in the west, too—for example, in Baden-Württemberg, a wealthy state home to much of the country’s automotive industry. In a sign of Germany’s greater manufacturing decline, the auto sector lost more than forty thousand jobs last year. The VW Group recently announced plans for fifty thousand additional phased layoffs and the end of production at four plants. That sort of malaise may lead to support for the AfD, even as it struggles with a solution. The Party’s co-chair Alice Weidel recently stumbled on television when asked to explain how German car producers could compete with growing demand for Chinese electric vehicles.
For years, the Brandmauer freed the AfD from such expectations. Yet competence at institutional defense is no substitute for an affirmative vision of governance. That’s also a lesson for other European democracies, from Austria to France, where mainstream parties have struggled to keep far-right challengers from power. A firewall can protect a political system, at least for a while, but it cannot explain what that system is for, or why its citizens should care. ♦

epub_13.title: Ric Burns, N.Y.C. Optimist
epub_13.text:
Ric Burns, N.Y.C. Optimist
Closeup Dept.
Ric Burns, N.Y.C. Optimist
The director—and brother of Ken Burns—is releasing two new episodes of his long-running “New York: A Documentary Film,” this time covering Superstorm Sandy,
COVID
, and Eric Adams.
By Eric Lach
September 12, 2026
Not long ago, the documentary filmmaker Ric Burns appeared in the doorway of his Upper West Side office with a fresh wound over his forehead. “You may wonder why I have a two-inch gash on my head,” he said, bowing to display the damage. Burns—the director of “New York: A Documentary Film”—had had a run-in with a metal paper-towel holder, to the tune of seven stitches. “Geysers of blood,” he said, entering a shadowy editing booth. “I got a photo if you want.”
Burns, the younger brother of fellow-filmmaker Ken Burns, was in the midst of making other bloody cuts: editing two long-gestating new episodes of “New York,” set to air later this month on PBS. One of his editors, Parker Dixon, sat at a console, staring at an iMac screen. The two began to work, Burns thinking aloud, Dixon cuing up footage. “Ric puts pen to paper,” Dixon said. “And from there we just feel it forward.”
Burns nodded. “It’s a funny balance,” he said. “Sometimes you want to be seeing what you hear, but a whole lot of times you don’t.”
Burns has worked out of the same offices overlooking Broadway and Seventy-third Street since 1989, two years before he and a collaborator, James Sanders, began work on “New York.” The first seven episodes, fourteen hours in all, aired between 1999 and 2001, covering everything from Henry Hudson’s first sail up the harbor to the city’s near-bankruptcy in the nineteen-seventies. An eighth episode, “The Center of the World,” three hours long, appeared in 2003, telling the story of the development and construction of the Twin Towers. The two new episodes, “Shadows of the Past” and “The Future of Cities,” cover the past fifty years. As Dixon browsed through shots of Jack Maple (the police official who pioneered CompStat), Michael Bloomberg being sworn in as mayor, Superstorm Sandy walloping the Manhattan and Brooklyn Bridges, footage of Times Square during
COVID
, and an interview with Eric Adams, Burns said that these were the trickiest installments he’s done. “It’s in the present,” he said. “It’s becoming history.”
How is it possible to make sense of a half century of booms and busts, rising and falling crime, skyrocketing inequality, terrorist attacks, waves of new immigrants, revolutionary technologies, divisive new politics, menacing new weather, protests, lockdowns, flowering countercultures, tragic and triumphant Knicks teams, and all the other elements of New York’s relentless change? “It’s staggering,” Burns said. “When it happens all around you in real time, you almost don’t realize it’s happening.”
The new episodes feature a Burnsian mix of carefully chosen images, lyrical voice-over, and cross-spectrum talking heads, including Bloomberg, the history scholar Kenneth T. Jackson, the feminist writer Carmen Boullosa, and the
Times
culture critic Wesley Morris. Check your doom loops at the door; Burns is a New York City optimist. “This is where the people are, it’s where the money is, it’s where the productivity is, it’s where the talent is, it’s where the creativity is,” he said. “People working hard at every conceivable kind of human enterprise.” For years, he has shot footage of pigeons swooping to and fro in the intersection below his office, known as Verdi Square. “I got a major thing for pigeons,” he said. “Pigeons are the New York animals, not rats.”
Editing is agony for Burns. He grimaced as Dixon skimmed through a segment about the twisty 2001 mayoral race which was being severely truncated. September 11th was a primary day in New York City. Until that morning, Bloomberg had trailed badly in the polls. After the planes hit, officials rescheduled the election. Bloomberg’s victory was arguably a bigger surprise than Zohran Mamdani’s win last year. One case that Burns makes implicitly in the new episodes is that Bloomberg, for all his administration’s faults and blind spots, will go down in history as the signal figure of early-twenty-first-century New York. “The only prior mayor who was a transformer like that was Fiorello LaGuardia,” Burns said. “And Bloomberg had the bigger challenge.”
Work on the new episodes began in earnest during the lockdown months of 2020, when the future of the city looked bleaker than it had at any time perhaps since the British imposed martial law, in 1776. But New York bounced back from
COVID
, as it had bounced back from Sandy, as it had bounced back from the Great Recession and the fiscal crisis. This resilience provides Burns with his great subject, and tracing its arcs has allowed him to connect the city’s past to its present. “Globalization arguably began when Henry Hudson rounded the corner of Coney Island, in 1609,” he said. “Fast-forward four hundred years, and here we are.” ♦

epub_14.title: Ke Huy Quan Keeps Smiling
epub_14.text:
Ke Huy Quan Keeps Smiling
Coming to America Dept.
Ke Huy Quan Keeps Smiling
On a trip to Liberty Island, the actor chats about his new memoir, “Never Say Die,” which chronicles his journey from refugee to child star in “Indiana Jones” to winning an Oscar, for “Everything Everywhere All at Once.”
By Sarah Larson
September 14, 2026
Before becoming a child movie star, in “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom” and “The Goonies,” the Oscar-winning actor Ke Huy Quan, born in Vietnam to ethnic-Chinese parents, lived with them and his eight siblings over his father’s plastic-bag factory, in Saigon. He emigrated with his father at age seven, starting with a harrowing boat trip to Hong Kong. He tells the boat story in a new memoir, “Never Say Die”—a “Goonies” reference—and thought of it again on a recent morning in lower Manhattan, as he boarded a ferry called the Miss Liberty. “This brings back memories of the Huey Fong, except that we were way more crowded,” Quan said, climbing the stairs. “And, instead of going up, we went down.” Tourists speaking several languages, some wearing foam Statue of Liberty crowns, filled the seats; Quan made his way to an upper-deck railing. He has kind eyes and a gently handsome face; his expressions tend toward earnest. As the ferry headed into the harbor, he gazed out at the Statue of Liberty, which he had never visited before. “I get a bit emotional thinking about this, and remembering some movie scenes that I’ve seen,” he said. “Especially ‘The Godfather Part II.’ ” He got quiet. “All the people coming here, hoping for an opportunity. I think if my dad was alive he’d be very proud.”
On Liberty Island, the path approaches the statue from behind, affording time to contemplate the folds of its enormous cloak. “I wonder what it was like transporting that across the ocean,” Quan said. Reaching the front, he beamed up at its majestic green head—“Ooh, look at that!”—and took a selfie, pointing, in a “Wow!” pose. He wore a black Uniqlo T-shirt of his own design, with yellow script that reads “Keep Smiling.” (Proceeds go to the U.N. Refugee Agency and the Displacement Film Fund.) “I’m going to post that to my I.G. later,” he said.
After arriving in the United States, Quan’s family reunited in Los Angeles’s Chinatown. One day in 1983, while he and his younger brother, David, were in E.S.L. class, they saw kids heading to an open-call movie audition at their school. David wanted to go, too, and Quan accompanied him, coaching him in Cantonese (“Bigger! Look at me—like this!”) and charming casting directors. Soon, Quan himself was at the Warner Bros. lot, auditioning before Harrison Ford, George Lucas, and Steven Spielberg, who cast him as the impishly heroic Short Round in “Temple of Doom.” (David was happy for him, Quan said.) “I didn’t know who they were,” Quan recalled, sitting on a wall. “I hadn’t seen ‘Star Wars’ or ‘Raiders of the Lost Ark.’ In fact, I’d never been to a movie theatre. The first time I went to a theatre and watched a movie with a live audience, I was in it.” In the memoir, he recalls the nurturing and kindness of Spielberg, and of Ford, who taught him how to swim. “ ‘Temple of Doom’ helped me kind of reshape what I went through as a kid in a positive way,” he said. “I was having fun and playing a character who was courageous and funny and really enjoying the ride, versus terrified and worried about surviving.” Behind him, tourists took photos with the statue; one happy teen posed like Lady Liberty, her arm raised, holding a novelty torch-shaped lemonade cup.
Seeing Quan, a young blond guy did a double take. “I literally was, like, Oh, my God, my favorite actor from ‘The Goonies’!” he said. Quan posed for some fan pictures, then headed to the lemonade stand. As a kid, he said, he’d loved being recognized, “but when my career went south”—subsequent roles were smaller, and he eventually worked as a creative consultant for Wong Kar-wai—he didn’t: “I thought I’d peaked at twelve.” (He did, however, meet his wife while working for Wong.) Since the release of “Everything Everywhere All at Once,” in 2022, for which he won the Oscar, “I am no longer uncomfortable,” he said. More good roles followed, including in last year’s “Zootopia 2.” “I play Gary De’Snake, a pit viper,” he said. “He may look intimidating, but he’s actually a kind and funny guy with a big heart.”
After a second ferry ride, Quan, sipping from his own torch-shaped lemonade cup, walked through the Ellis Island museum. “So this is the building where all the immigrants came through!” he said, in the sunny hall. He admired sepia-toned photos of immigrant kids holding American flags (“What an incredible thing America did”) and took in exhibits about restrictions and bigotry. He peered at some cartoons from 1882. “The first group of Chinese immigrants to this country were lied to—they ended up doing hard labor,” he said. “I would love to do a movie about that one day.” ♦

epub_15.title: Paula Cole Doesn’t Want to Wait
epub_15.text:
Paula Cole Doesn’t Want to Wait
Comeback Dept.
Paula Cole Doesn’t Want to Wait
At the Conservatory Garden, the singer reflects on her new two-album set, “Sonic Memoir: Demos 1989-1998”; launching Lilith Fair with Sarah McLachlan; and the time Jay Leno made fun of her armpit hair.
By Rachel Syme
September 14, 2026
The 1998 Grammy Awards should have been a triumphant night for the singer-songwriter Paula Cole. She was nominated for seven awards for her second album, “This Fire,” including Producer of the Year, Non-Classical, an honor that has yet to go to a woman (a factoid that she calls “deeply fucked”). That night, Cole, then twenty-nine, performed “Where Have All the Cowboys Gone?” and won Best New Artist, beating out Hanson, Erykah Badu, Fiona Apple, and Puff Daddy. Yet all anyone could talk about, afterward, was the sight of Cole’s unshaven armpits at the ceremony. On “The Tonight Show,” Jay Leno trotted out a Cole doll and shined his shoes with its copious pit hair. When
Entertainment Weekly
airbrushed out her fuzz, Cole called the magazine “cowardly.” “If I look back,” she said the other day, “I see myself just nose-diving into unhappiness. I felt like prey. There was a deadening behind my eyes.”
Cole, who is now fifty-eight and has an Earth Mother vibe—baggy jeans, chore coat, beaded necklaces, orange Hokas—was sitting in the Conservatory Garden in Central Park. She had come, as she put it, “to commune with pollinators” before kicking off a national tour marking the thirtieth anniversary of “This Fire.” She views the tour, along with the release of a new two-album set called “Sonic Memoir: Demos 1989-1998,” as a chance to reclaim the idealistic artist she was before the music business chewed her up. “After my third record, I had a complete nervous breakdown on tour in Germany,” she said. Although she stepped away from the industry, she never stopped working, quietly releasing eight more records, including two that she funded through Kickstarter. “I have found solace in being independent and not working with labels anymore,” she said. “I get to keep the music pure.” She survives mostly on royalties from her 1997 single “I Don’t Want to Wait,” which became the theme song to “Dawson’s Creek.” “That song is like Robin Hood,” she said. “I take that money and put it into my lesser-known art.”
She is still astounded by the fascination with her grooming preferences. “I was just this small-town girl,” she said, shaking her silver hair, which she’d braided and pinned across her head, milkmaid style. Going au naturel was an extension of her bohemian upbringing in coastal Massachusetts, where her mother worked as an artist, and where her father was a biology professor and the bass player in a polka band. “Music was a living language in our house,” she said, then tilted her head. “Listen to them!” she said, referring to some chirping crickets. “They are sending out messages to each other, like ‘O.K., it’s the end of the season, the light is changing. We better mate and propagate.’ ” She went on,“My dad studied entomology. I think we need to befriend insects. They are the largest kingdom existing on Earth, and we are fucking it up. We’re dusting our crops with glyphosates. We’re destroying soil. We import compost. It’s completely illogical, and we’re headed for a breakdown.”
Cole splits her time between Manhattan and ten acres in Massachusetts, where she cultivates the land. A few years back, she discovered a book called “The Resilient Farm and Homestead,” by the naturalist Ben Falk, and became a convert to his “permaculture” philosophy. Cole dug rainwater swales, installed a woodstove, and planted vegetables. (She hasn’t eaten meat since she was fourteen.) This summer, she visited Falk’s farm in Vermont, where she worked alongside hippies half her age. “I came screeching in as this old city person,” she said. “I had to share a bathroom with nine men, which was really hard-core. Everyone was barefoot, just slipping in and out of their Crocs, and I was, like, ew. But I overcame that, and started putting my feet on the land. You feel your bones spread out. It’s fantastic.”
Cole strolled along a path lined with daylilies and Japanese anemones. She smiled at a sculpture of a boy and a girl from Frances Hodgson Burnett’s “The Secret Garden.” “It has never been easy to be a woman in the public eye,” she said. Cole was instrumental in launching Lilith Fair, in 1997. “I’d opened for Sarah McLachlan,” she said. “Every night I’d go out and I would thank her for having a female opener, because it just didn’t happen. Promoters said women don’t sell tickets.”
Turning back to the new record, she said, “I cringe when I listen to some of those old recordings. I’m out of tune, and it’s messy. But the whole idea of it was for the fans to hear the process of me arriving at myself as a producer and as a human.” On tour, she will sing “This Fire” in the original key. “I’m postmenopausal and my voice has changed,” she said. “But I refuse to lose an octave.” ♦

epub_16.title: The Hearing Aid That Plays It by Ear
epub_16.text:
The Hearing Aid That Plays It by Ear
Brave New World
The Hearing Aid That Plays It by Ear
A company called Fortell made an A.I.-powered device that tries to tune out background noise in real time. Does it work? Ask Fortell’s test subject, Steve Martin.
By David Owen
September 14, 2026
In 2023, the comedian, actor, writer, and banjo virtuoso Steve Martin was walking through SoHo, followed closely by two men holding a laptop. The laptop was connected by an Ethernet cable to a 3-D-printed plastic box, and the box was connected by wires to Martin’s head. A passerby recognized him and asked whether the benefits of celebrity included having assistants literally tethered to him. But the men with the laptop weren’t working for Martin. They were engineers, and Martin was serving as a beta tester for an invention of theirs, a new kind of hearing aid. The men referred to the laptop as the “diesel-powered” version of their device, which they were hoping to refine, then shrink. Late last year, with continuing help from Martin and others, they succeeded. Their company is called Fortell. Its inaugural hearing-aid-fitting clinic is at Sixty-first and Park. Their waiting room is decorated with paintings that Martin (without assistance) brought from his collection.
“We started crude and got better,” Matthew de Jonge, one of Fortell’s four co-founders, said not long ago, in the waiting area. “The thing that’s novel about our hearing aid is that it filters out sound that, in our estimation, is unimportant and thus distracting, and it does it in real time.”
In bars, clubs, and other loud, crowded places, young people almost always hear better than old people. One reason is that the un-degraded auditory circuitry in their heads is able to zero in on the people they’re trying to hook up with while blocking out everyone else, a minor superpower known as the cocktail-party effect. “As people lose hearing, they also become less capable of listening selectively,” Cole Morris, another Fortell co-founder, said. Modern hearing aids have some ability to compensate, by using directional microphones and conventional noise cancellation. “They’re pretty good at dialling down so-called stationary sounds, like the hum of an air-conditioner,” de Jonge said. “What they have never been able to do is to separate speech you want to hear from speech you don’t, and to do it even if the speech you don’t want to hear is louder than the speech you do.”
De Jonge and Morris were roommates at Princeton, and later de Jonge was among the creators of Butterfly iQ, an A.I.-enhanced handheld medical-imaging device that is now one of the best-selling sonogram systems in the world. (It was used on the International Space Station to evaluate an astronaut who was later evacuated, and it has appeared in a supporting role in episodes of “The Pitt.”) Early in the Butterfly project, the team received an e-mail from a professor at Harvard, who told de Jonge that he was working with the best physics-Ph.D. student he’d ever had. “He said the guy’s field was quantum optics, whatever that is, but that what he really wanted to do was A.I. for health care,” de Jonge recalled. “He said the guy had no experience in either A.I. or health care but asked if I would hire him. I said yes.”
The physics Ph.D. was Igor Lovchinsky, a Russian émigré. “There are special Russian music schools, and I was admitted to one of them when I was four,” he said. He moved to the United States with his family, won a scholarship to Juilliard, and became a celebrated concert pianist, before switching to physics. He designed Butterfly’s neural networks, then did the same for Fortell, of which he is also a co-founder. The fourth co-founder, Andrew Casper, designed the custom chips used in both projects. Fortell’s hearing aids sell for sixty-eight hundred dollars per pair, about average for the top of the line.
Paul Krawitz is a sixty-seven-year-old retired ophthalmic surgeon in Cold Spring Harbor, on Long Island. He first realized he had a hearing problem ten years ago. “When my bedroom windows were open, I could hear the crickets in my yard if my right ear was on the pillow, but not when I rolled over,” he said. He tried six different hearing aids, but wasn’t happy with any of them. “I was a pain in the ass as an audiology patient,” he said. “I wanted cognitively transparent improvement in my hearing, not just an increase in volume.”
He made an appointment at Fortell on a whim. “A typical audiologist will sit on the other side of the room and ask, ‘How do I sound?,’ ” he said. “But the Fortell audiologist said she was going to take me on a field trip.” They conversed out on the sidewalk, with Manhattan traffic in the background, then visited an espresso bar. “I heard beautifully,” he said. “You know, the ability to pass naturally in conversation is not a luxury. It’s fundamental to human connection.” Krawitz noticed another difference at home, while listening to Rachmaninoff’s Second Symphony. “People who love music sometimes refer to hearing the ‘air’ between the players, and for the first time in many years I heard it again,” he said. “My wife goes, ‘Why are you crying?’ ” ♦

epub_18.title: The Incredible Journey of a Migratory Shorebird
epub_18.text:
The Incredible Journey of a Migratory Shorebird
Dept. of Science
The Incredible Journey of a Migratory Shorebird
Godwits make the longest non-stop migration in the bird world. That might be the least of their marvels. Can they survive a changing planet?
By Rivka Galchen
September 14, 2026
On a sunny June morning, in a bog outside Beluga, Alaska, I met a Hudsonian godwit. She had inky eyes and a long, slightly upturned beak that was pinkish-orange at its base and brownish-black at its tip. The feathers on her back were of mottled sepia tones, and those on her belly were rusty brown and painterly white. Her legs reminded me of the slender inserts of spring-loaded ballpoint pens, and her feet were refined pterodactyl claws. Her name (among humans) was A34, and she was about the size of a city pigeon. She was in the hands of Nathan Senner, a conservation biologist, who removed and replaced her geotag; measured her head, beak, wing, and leg; weighed her; and took two tail feathers and a sample of her blood. From that small number of data points, he can deduce where she’s been, how her feathers have grown, what genetic subgroup she belongs to, and her degree of exposure to mercury.
Senner leads a research laboratory at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, that is largely focussed on how migratory shorebirds, such as godwits, respond to environmental change. He grew up in Anchorage, where school loudspeakers announced the street corners on which moose had been sighted. In high school, he wrote an occasional “Birding with Nathan” column for the Anchorage
Daily News
. Senner’s father, Stanley, has devoted more than five decades to the conservation of migratory shorebirds. Starting in the nineteen-seventies, Stanley and his colleagues have been sounding the alarm on the vulnerability of shorebirds and working to protect key habitats, such as Alaska’s Copper River Delta. “Back then, no one was even talking about climate change,” he told me recently. Since 1980, roughly half of migratory shorebird species’ populations have declined by more than fifty per cent.
Migratory shorebirds are usually not a person’s first bird crush. They lack the supernatural aura of the resplendent quetzal, and they don’t go in for outlandish mating displays like that of the prairie chicken. As the Princeton University biology professor and shorebird-lover David Wilcove put it, migratory shorebirds can give an impression of being “little brown guys, buzzing around in the mud, not too big and not too small, and, whether one is a stint or a phalarope or a knot or a godwit, they’re just kind of there.” And yet, Wilcove told me, they are a birder’s kind of bird. Once people get to know them, they tend to fall in love.
Relatively few people have laid eyes on Hudsonian godwits. The birds mostly divide their time between remote northern bogs and muddy South American shores. John James Audubon apparently never saw a living one; he based his drawing of them in “Birds of America” on a few specimens he found in markets. Arthur Cleveland Bent, in a 1927 installment of his twenty-one-volume series, “Life Histories of North American Birds,” wrote of Hudsonian godwits, “I can count on the fingers of one hand the red-letter days when I have been privileged to see this rare and handsome wader.”
It’s entirely possible that I had encountered A34 two months before seeing her in Alaska. In March, I had travelled from New York to Chiloé Island, in Chilean Patagonia. Flocks of Hudsonian godwits (the smallest of the four godwit species and the least well known) spend from roughly early October to April in and around the tidal mudflats there. The island also has Humboldt penguins, giant rhubarb plants with leaves as large as umbrellas, and the world’s smallest species of deer. Castro, the main town, is famous for its brightly painted wooden seaside houses, which rest on tall stilts to accommodate the tide.
Homo sapiens
is a shore-loving species. About forty per cent of us live within sixty miles of a coast.
Chiloé is where Hudsonian godwits spend their non-breeding season and express their non-breeding personality, which is intensely gregarious and food-oriented. If you walk at low tide on the mudflats of Pullao Bay, you will see godwits bobbing for bivalves and worms, dunking their beaks in and out of the ground as if they were darning. They share their feasting grounds with oystercatchers, ducks, whimbrels, greater yellowlegs and lesser yellowlegs, and other shorebirds that neither I nor my Merlin Bird ID app could identify. The longer I watched the shorebirds on Chiloé Island, the stronger my impression was that they were dressed for a masquerade or a carnival, with some wearing stout beaks, some slim ones, others elegantly curved ones. The pale bellies and darker backs of many of the birds made it look as if they had on fashionable capes over slender, hosiery-clad legs. They called out to one another and occasionally broke into cotillion-like flight. The Hudsonian godwits appeared eternally committed to these revels. There was no sign that they were about to fly nearly ten thousand miles to Alaska, a wondrous and mystifying migration that one scientist called “technically impossible.”
Birds are in trouble. Migratory shorebirds are in especially bad trouble. And
long-distance
migratory shorebirds, like the Hudsonian godwit, may be in the most trouble. “Birds are sentinels,” Stanley Senner told me. “The ecosystems they rely on are ecosystems we rely on as well, though it can take time to convince people of that.” Studies show that, without shorebirds, coastlines erode more quickly, trap less carbon, and are more likely to become unbalanced. In the Yellow Sea, for example, shorebirds feed on crabs whose population needs to be kept in check, as they graze on native vegetation. In some ways, shorebirds are analogous to the wolves that hunt the deer and elk populations that eat the tree saplings that become the trees that beavers use to build dams that help the fish—and so on. Shorebirds also transport and disperse essential seeds and nutrients. Our interests align, as they say. Also, like all birds, they are lovable, alien, awesome, and alive. Not long ago, I saw a dead magpie on a country highway. Other magpies gathered around it, as if saddened and confused. When a car approached, they scattered. After the car passed, they returned to their fallen friend. So there’s also that.
To protect birds effectively, we need to understand them. So much about godwits remains unknown, including where and when they encounter their most mortal threats. Since their epic migration is maybe their most difficult-to-fathom characteristic, we may as well start there.
The story of bird migration, as narrated in Western civilization, often begins with Aristotle, who wrote that, in the winter, redstarts turn into robins and garden warblers turn into blackcaps. This sounds silly but, compared with the idea that a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, it seems reasonable. Olaus Magnus, a sixteenth-century Swedish priest, argued that barn swallows disappear in the fall because they hibernate at the bottom of ponds. That also seems absurd until you learn about the common poorwill, which resembles an old piece of bark and spends months of winter nestled almost imperceptibly in the crevices of logs or among piles of rocks. This wasn’t scientifically documented until 1948, although the poorwill has long been known to the Hopi as
hölchoko
, “the sleeping one.”
The Maori tell a story about how a godwit showed their ancestors the way from their ancient homeland of Hawaiki to New Zealand, more than a thousand miles away. But, to most people, avian migrations of that length were long unimaginable. In 1822, a hunter near the German town of Klütz shot down a stork; when he collected the bird, he saw that it had a wooden spear through its neck, later determined to be of African origin. Hunters eventually found more such
Pfeilstorchs
(arrow storks), giving credence to the hypothesis that the white stork not only migrated but did so between Europe and Africa. In some ways, this was a downgrade: the seventeenth-century minister Charles Morton, who wrote a popular physics textbook, claimed that birds migrated to the moon. He supposed that they fuelled a sixty-day flight there with body fat (reasonable) and that the journey was made easier by the minimal atmospheric resistance in space (also reasonable).
Migratory birds in captivity develop
Zugunruhe,
an agitated fitfulness, at certain times of year. Scientists don’t know precisely what provoked A34 to set off northward one spring afternoon, with a flock of her fellows, though, if they did, they might better know how her species will be affected by the shifting seasons of our changing climate. Godwits cannot soar like hawks or glide like albatrosses. They migrate by continuously flapping their wings. They must navigate crosswinds and headwinds, storms and maybe an occasional hurricane, continuing on day after day, night after night. As best as we can tell, they do not, while flying, eat or drink or sleep (at least not with more than one hemisphere of their brain at a time). After a journey of hundreds of hours and thousands of miles, they descend on a snow-covered shore at the Cook Inlet of southern Alaska or another favored breeding ground. They land considerably lighter than when they took off. “Many arriving shorebirds seem to be tired,” the ornithologist and conservationist Joseph Archibald Hagar wrote, in his foundational monograph, “Nesting of the Hudsonian Godwit at Churchill, Manitoba,” from 1966. In a field-diary entry, Hagar describes a group of birds that “within a minute or two dropped into some sunny spot out of the wind, tucked heads into scapulars, and went to sleep, not to move again for as long as we watched.”
In 1976, the young ornithologist Robert Gill took a job with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in Anchorage. He was dispatched to the Alaska Peninsula to do biological inventories on public land that was up for lease to private companies. During those long-lit Alaskan summer days, walking across salt marshes and through the foothills of the mountains, Gill encountered thousands upon thousands of migratory shorebirds. He told me, “In Alaska, where the seasons are so prominent, it’s very dramatic. It feels like all the birds turn up over the course of one weekend in May.” Along with godwits, the peninsula was a summer home to yellowlegs, dowitchers, sandpipers, Arctic terns, and other species. But almost no one was aware that so many birds relied on this land. How the birds managed their journeys, where they might stop along the way, even how many of them there were—no one knew for sure. “In the vast expanses of wetlands and coastal tundra, you could see why,” Gill said.
The extinction of the once common passenger pigeon, famously described by the naturalist John Muir in his memoir (“I have seen flocks streaming south in the fall so large that they were flowing over from horizon to horizon in an almost continuous stream all day long, at the rate of forty or fifty miles an hour, like a mighty river in the sky”), was part of the impetus behind the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918. Godwits are protected under the act, so killing them or holding them captive, even for scientific purposes, is highly regulated. Also, they’re difficult to capture. Gill’s means of learning more about them was limited, he said, to “the kind of observational work done by old-school naturalists.”
In October of 1987, Gill received a call about nine bar-tailed godwits that had crashed into a radar dome near Cold Bay, Alaska, and died. “They were greaseballs,” he recalled. “They made any Christmas goose look lean.” The carcasses were sent to a lab to be analyzed. Fifty-five per cent of their body mass turned out to be fat. Gill suspected that these chubby godwits were preparing to fly non-stop from Alaska to New Zealand, where this species wintered. However, at that time, the longest known non-stop migration flight was barely half that long. “But, if they were going to stop in French Polynesia, why carry all that baggage?” Gill reasoned.
The lab also measured the birds’ internal organs. Gill’s collaborator, Theunis Piersma, noticed something peculiar: the guts, gizzard, liver, and kidneys of these birds were very small—it was like cutting open a lion and encountering digestive organs the size of a house cat’s. Then, in March of 1992, some forty godwit carcasses were seized from a poacher in New Zealand. These were birds in a very different part of their migratory cycle, and their digestive organs, when analyzed, were of more normal proportions. In 1998, Piersma and Gill published their findings in a paper titled “Guts Don’t Fly: Small Digestive Organs in Obese Bar-Tailed Godwits,” concluding that the birds shrank their digestive organs to reduce their weight and their metabolic demands during a non-stop migration. And then, somehow, regrew them.
This conclusion remained debatable. For one thing, Gill and Piersma had no direct evidence that the birds flew without stopping. At the time, there were no tags sufficiently lightweight for tracking birds as small as godwits. But transmitters kept shrinking, and, in 2007, Gill flew to New Zealand, where, after a lot of patient, muddy field work, he succeeded in putting tags on sixteen bar-tailed godwits. The trackers could send signals to satellites to pinpoint the birds’ location. By today’s norms, the trackers were pretty heavy. Many of them failed within months, but one lasted much longer than expected.
A female godwit, E7, took off on March 17, 2007, from near the Piako River, on New Zealand’s North Island. She flew more than six thousand miles non-stop to a nature preserve on the Yalu River, near the China-North Korea border; she stayed there for a little more than a month; she arrived at her nesting area in Alaska on May 15th and spent the summer there. The tracker was still working on August 29th, when E7 started flying southeast, over the Pacific. Gill’s team was doing field work in western Alaska and had only spotty internet service; the team would gather around a laptop, waiting for the updates on E7’s location to come through. North of Kauai, she took a slight right turn and continued flying. On September 7th, after more than two hundred hours aloft, she landed at the mouth of the Piako River, back on the North Island of New Zealand, where Gill had first met her.
Before E7, the longest documented non-stop migratory-bird flight was that of a Far Eastern curlew who had flown about four thousand miles. E7 flew some seven thousand without a break. The flight defied reason. “I had an engineering professor at M.I.T. call me up and say he gave his students an assignment to compare the size and flight range of E7 to a 747 jet,” Gill said.
How these birds could put on so much fat and still be healthy remains somewhat mysterious. “The dogma for mammals is that fat is good fuel for low-intensity exercise—but the flapping flight required for migration is thought to be pretty high intensity,” Maria Stager, an evolutionary biologist at UMass, Amherst, who studies the physiology of songbirds, told me. Marathoners consume sugary carbohydrate-rich gels, not bacon bits. Stager is Nathan Senner’s wife; she assists him in his field work, and he assists her in hers. A couple of years ago, to better understand godwit migration, they began a collaboration with Chris Guglielmo, a professor of biology at Ontario’s Western University and the director of its Centre for Animals on the Move, where he often uses wind tunnels to measure birds’ flight dynamics and metabolism. A wind tunnel works much like those “endless” swimming pools, in which you stay in place while swimming against a current. But the wind tunnel wouldn’t work for godwits. “If I tried to get a bird to fly non-stop for eleven days in my wind tunnel—well, first of all, I don’t think my animal-care committee would approve of it, because the bird would probably die of dehydration,” he said.
Guglielmo had done the math. “We knew how fat the birds got,” he said. “We knew the energy content of fat and nonfat tissue.” According to these measurements, even the fattest of the birds would run out of fuel—body fat and a bit of muscle—after about twenty-five hundred miles. “So not even halfway,” he said.
Guglielmo played around a bit with such variables as drag coefficient and presumed altitude. He eventually came up with parameters in which birds might survive flying six thousand miles non-stop—but only if they could complete the journey in four or five days. Tracking data showed that the migrations were never that brief. “They shouldn’t be able to go seven, nine, eleven days,” Guglielmo said. And yet they did. “They look diminutive, fragile, and delicate. But they’re these high-performance Ferrari machines.”
He had a hypothesis about what was going on. Hummingbirds can save energy by going into torpor at night, lowering their body temperature and their heart rate. Little brown bats can similarly reduce their metabolic demands by going Dracula for months at a time, decreasing their body temperatures by more than fifty degrees Fahrenheit and slowing their respiration to a handful of breaths an hour. Guglielmo wondered whether godwits did something similar, even though hanging motionless in a torpor seems pretty different from flying.
But there were no data on the heart rate and body temperature of migrating godwits. So, in the summer of 2024, Guglielmo joined Stager and Senner during their field work in Beluga. With him were the veterinarian Beverly Chua, a postdoctoral student named Catherine Ivy, and a graduate student, Kevin Young. When Senner and Stager caught a godwit, they would pass it along to Guglielmo and Young, who would drive the bird to a makeshift operating room they had set up at their lodge. Chua would put it to sleep with isoflurane, intubate it, cover its eyes to keep them from drying out, make a small incision in its abdomen to insert a device that would log heart rate and body temperature, and then sew the bird up. The surgery took about twenty minutes. From the birds’ perspective, Guglielmo said, “it must feel like an alien abduction.”
“In total, we placed the trackers in ten birds, five males and five females,” Guglielmo told me. Whether they would see those individuals again was uncertain; the birds would have to survive the summer, fly down to Chiloé Island, survive there, fly back to Beluga, and be recaptured. “When I look at them, I have this little moment and think, They’re going to go off and do these amazing things,” Guglielmo said. The following summer, the team returned, as did at least nine of the ten godwits. The data extracted from the trackers are being analyzed, a slow process.
When I flew into Beluga, on a four-seat Cessna, my bird’s-eye view was of blue-and-green water that softly transitioned into brown-and-green land. The pilot pointed out gray harbor seals and some of the village’s namesake pink-white whales. The two other passengers were working on a project to keep the local Chinook and coho salmon, which are essential to the area’s commercial-fishing industry, from being decimated by the northern pike, an invasive species that preys on the salmon. Beluga, with a permanent human population of thirty-four, is visited by duck hunters, fishermen, oil workers, solar contractors, U.S. Geological Survey scientists, and Senner’s team of ornithological researchers, who come each year to monitor the nesting grounds.
“As extraordinary as their migration is, maybe it has led us to overlook other aspects of their life cycle,” Senner told me one evening. “We have this idea that migration is dangerous and that a lot of birds are likely dying in migration,” he went on. “That’s born in part from the fact that we do occasionally see these mass-mortality events.” A powerful tornado off the coast of Louisiana in 1993 killed three humans and tens of thousands of birds, most of them neotropical migrants—orioles, warblers, thrushes, vireos—who were nearing the end of their migration across the Gulf of Mexico. In the fall of 2020, following droughts and a cold snap in the American Southwest, estimates suggest that more than a hundred thousand migrating birds died—many of them falling directly out of the sky.
“But what we’ve been finding with migratory shorebirds suggests the opposite,” Senner went on. “Migration is
not
necessarily the most dangerous time of the year.” José A. Alves, at the University of East Anglia, led a team that compared two groups of Icelandic black-tailed godwits. The godwits that wintered farther away, in Portugal, actually fared better than those that wintered in England. “When we think about conservation, we need to think about where in their life cycle they are most vulnerable,” Senner said.
About a hundred and fifty Hudsonian godwit pairs breed in the bogs near Beluga. After a post-migratory rest, courting begins with aerobatic displays by the males, which involve butterfly-like flapping followed by free-fall nosedives from which they gracefully pull out at the last second. The females lead “pursuit flights,” in which they fly swiftly, with abrupt tilts and turns; a male partner follows just behind and below. Sometimes females stay with last year’s partner, sometimes they choose a new partner. Unchosen males, known (alas!) as “failed males,” spend the season flying around in a group, seemingly to harass paired males and to impress paired females.
A godwit couple will scrape a few shallow, saucer-shaped indentations (sometimes referred to as “nest cups”) into a grassy spot, select one of them, and proceed to nest as imperceptibly as possible. Parents sit atop their clutch of eggs (almost always four) on a predictable schedule: the females from about 6
A.M.
to 6
P.M.
and the males for the remaining twelve hours, with each bird of the couple feeding at the shore in their off-nest time. These four eggs are usually the birds’ one hope during the whole year of producing offspring; the festive godwits of Chiloé become, in the breeding grounds, measured, quiet, and focussed. Nesting is always perilous, but the moment when the male and female trade places is especially so, as the incubating bird’s movement may catch the attention of a predator.
The bogs in late May are a vast expanse of hummocks of yellowed sedge interspersed with small ponds and copses of black spruce where moose like to hang out. Underfoot, the bog is squishy and resilient, with unseen holes here and there. It gets softer and sinkier as spring advances. Wearing thigh-high rubber boots, I spent three days in this landscape, tramping behind Stager and Senner as they sought out nest sites, tracked the progress of eggs, and weighed, measured, and tagged expecting parents.
It was here that Senner handed A34 to me for a moment. She was warmer than I expected a bird to be. I could feel her heartbeat. When I was in elementary school, I briefly shared an elevator with the actor Robert Wagner, whom I recognized from the TV show “Hart to Hart.” He caught my eye and said hello. The encounter was otherworldly and wondrous. Holding A34 felt something like that. Then I opened my hands and she took off, back to her clutch of eggs, which, if not eaten by a coyote or a sandhill crane or another hungry creature, would soon hatch. Life is stressful for Hudsonian godwits: Senner told me that, across godwit studies, he has never seen a rate of chicks surviving to fledging higher than about twenty-five per cent.
Senner began collecting data from godwit nesting sites in Beluga in 2009, when Robert Gill helped him to scout out the terrain. Godwit couples maintain large territories, establishing nests far from other godwits. They prefer dense boggy areas that tend to keep humans away. Their nests are built in existing sedge clumps, with minimal modifications, and are therefore ridiculously hard to find—as Gill put it, they’re “very cryptic,” even for expert eyes. Senner is known for having a “nest sense,” but, as he said, “all that ends up meaning is that rather than spending twenty-four walking hours per nest find, I spend maybe twelve.”
One of the more reliable approaches to nest-finding is to follow a male godwit returning to take over nighttime duties. Late one afternoon, Senner and Stager separately staked out two males. They each waited for about three hours. The godwit males remained in spruce treetops, give or take an occasional short flight. Either the birds were on to them, or they were failed males with no nests to fly back to.
That godwits reproduce at all is astounding. They must shuttle great distances between southern and northern latitudes of the globe, figuring out not only the location of their breeding grounds but the optimal moment to arrive so that their eggs can hatch when insects are at their most abundant. Between 1974 and 2010, godwits were arriving earlier than usual, by as much as nine days. Was this an adaptation to a changing climate? Maybe, but, between 2011 and 2023, the godwits’ arrival date shifted again, to as many as six days
later
. “I used to be able to say, ‘Come up here on June 1st and you will definitely see chicks hatch,’ ” Senner told me. “But I can’t really say that anymore.” This second shift seemed counterintuitive and maladaptive, since peak insect abundance is directly related to snowmelt. “One of the closest correlations to arrival date is when spring came the previous year, which makes it seem like the birds remember that,” Senner said. With climate change, the bogs are drying out, so there are fewer insects for young chicks to eat. Yet more nests are hatching, even as a smaller percentage of those chicks are surviving.
Stager recalled a long evening she and Senner once spent looking for nests: “This beautiful thunderstorm was approaching, and we were, like, ‘We should not be in this open bog right now, but also we need to be banding these chicks.’ ” They were searching near where a male godwit was resting in a treetop, indicating a nest nearby, but they were having no luck finding it. Then the male began “making these horrible distressed calls that I’ve never heard another bird make,” Stager said. She and Senner spotted a northern harrier. Their approach startled the predator, who took off with the mother godwit in its claws. When the father flew down to his chicks, Stager and Senner managed to catch and tag all the birds—“He was pretty angry with us,” Stager said—then retreated from the stormy bog. The father was left to tend to the chicks himself until they were old enough to survive on their own. At least two of those four chicks survived, Senner told me. He knew because those birds returned to Beluga a couple of years later. “Usually, even with two parents, very few chicks make it,” he said. “I thought, Wow, he is a really great dad.”
Chicks can walk within a few hours of hatching, but it’s several more weeks before they can fly. By the end of this year’s breeding season, about twenty per cent of the hatched chicks had fledged. It was a good year. In one nest, three of four chicks survived. In some other nests, no chick lived beyond a week. One of A34’s chicks survived. On my last afternoon in Beluga, Stager told me, “I don’t consider myself a conservation biologist like Nate—it would make me too sad.”
Godwit parents brood their chicks, alert them to danger, lead them to hiding places, and (in a dramatic and short-lived personality shift) aggressively squawk at and harry their potential predators. Then, in July, the adults begin their southward migration, leaving their young behind. Although much remains unknown about godwits in general, even more remains unknown about the juveniles. They have been observed leaving Alaska in August and September, though it’s unclear how they find their way. Hudsonian juveniles have now and again been spotted in New Zealand and Australia, rather than in South America, among flocks of bar-tailed godwits. More recently, the scientists Juan G. Navedo and Jorge Ruiz, from the Universidad Austral de Chile, tagged some birds in Chiloé and discovered that, instead of travelling to Alaska in the spring to breed, they spent the boreal summer in the pampas of Argentina.
Sixty years ago, the naturalist and writer Peter Matthiessen observed in this magazine that the Hudsonian godwit was among the most precarious of the North American shorebirds: “It is an exceptionally unassertive bird, readily chivied by marbled godwits, and even sanderlings. Was it always so timid, or is the degeneration brought about by mutation? Has it become specialized in some way not yet understood? . . . The naturalist who could find answers to such questions would explain a good deal that we do not know about ecology and ethology and genetics.”
Money and political will being scarce resources, questions of where and when to apply them are the constant companions of conservation science. The long-term survival of Hudsonian godwits—and migratory shorebirds more broadly—depends to a significant degree on scientists figuring out what efforts will be most effective. “I hate to say it, but you might call it an optimization problem,” Nathan Senner told me.
“Tidal mudflats have suffered from not being perceived as beautiful sights,” Wilcove, of Princeton, said. The dun-colored flats often stretch for miles. “The degradation of a tidal flat is not as apparent as the clear-cutting of a forest or the damming of a river,” he went on. “It just looks like a place you don’t want to walk, because it’s really hot and you could sink down to your waist. It’s hard for people to imagine that it’s an incredibly vibrant and important habitat for so much wildlife.”
The Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network, founded in 1985, initially focussed on setting up what Stanley Senner described as “a string of pearls” consisting of wetlands along migratory routes, with Alaska’s Copper River Delta becoming one of the first of more than a hundred designated sites. “But now we’re coming to understand that it’s not enough,” Senner said. Smaller-scale interventions also do essential work. In California, for example, rice farmers are paid to flood their fields during key weeks of the year, for the use of migrating birds. W.H.S.R.N. has collaborative conservation projects at sites up and down the Americas, including at ranches in Uruguay, salt ponds in Ecuador, and shrimp farms in Honduras. In Chiloé, Senner’s colleague Natalia Martínez-Curci, of Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council, has spent years working with the local aquaculture industry, along with members of the Indigenous community, who recently built a bird observatory.
But, of course, migratory shorebirds aren’t limited to the Western Hemisphere. Scientists studying the East Asian-Australasian Flyway (which runs roughly from Alaska and Siberia down to New Zealand and Australia) spent time trying to identify what the various migratory bird species in steepest decline had in common. Was it body size? Breeding range? Migratory distance? The shared variable turned out to be reliance on the coastal wetlands of China’s Yellow Sea. Between 1980 and 2014, about a third of that coastline was lost to land reclamation. Tong Mu, a thirty-five-year-old researcher at Princeton, said that when he began his graduate work on migratory shorebirds of the flyway, in 2014, “everything seemed very gloomy to me, and to many people.” Mu did his Ph.D. under Wilcove, working to identify which parts of the Yellow Sea flats were most used by birds.
In 2018, following much clamoring by scientists, the Chinese government enacted strict restrictions on commercial land reclamation along its coast. In 2019, parts of the Yellow Sea mudflats were named a
UNESCO
World Heritage site. “I would say that the government realized that sustainable development and ecological conservation are a very important part of the story that they want to tell,” Mu said. He recalled doing field work with a much older researcher who said, half joking, half complaining, that science and conservation have nothing to do with each other—that, regardless of how excellent the science is, policymakers will only hear what they want to hear. “But I think science is still very important,” Mu said.
I asked him for his impression of what migratory shorebirds are like—what his sense was of their personalities, if it was even O.K. to use the word “personality” in relation to birds. He was quiet for a moment. “Sorry, it makes me a little emotional to talk about it,” he said, smiling. Mu spent five Arctic summers in far-eastern Russia, where mating pairs each have their own territory. He grew more attached to them in that setting, witnessing their individual dramas. “There are some success stories,” he said. “But also many failures. The birds’ nests may be depredated. Or they may have terrible weather, and the chicks can’t survive it. And, you know, they have travelled thousands of kilometres, just for that.”
Mu recalled placing a young chick under his hat, to keep the bird warm while he prepared to tag it. “When they are very young, they cannot maintain their body temperature, and have to be covered by the adults every now and then,” he said. The chick called out in distress. An adult bird flew over, landing on Mu’s head. He took off the hat, and the adult dove in after the chick. ♦
